title: Inverse Functions
learningObjective: Find the inverse of a one-to-one function.

faqs.question: What is an inverse function, and what does it mean for one function to "undo" another?
faqs.answer:
An inverse function reverses whatever the original function did. If f takes an input and produces an output, the inverse takes that same output and hands you back the original input. Formally, f has an inverse g when f(g(x)) = x and g(f(x)) = x for every x — plugging one into the other, in either order, just gets you back to where you started.
Example

Converting Fahrenheit to Celsius, and Celsius back to Fahrenheit, are inverses of each other: each one exactly undoes what the other one did.

faqs.question: What is the notation for an inverse function, and how is f⁻¹(x) different from 1/f(x)?
faqs.answer: An inverse function is written f⁻¹(x), read "f inverse of x." This is a completely different thing from 1/f(x) — the −1 here is not an exponent, even though it looks like one. f⁻¹(x) means "the inverse function," while 1/f(x) means "one divided by f(x)." These are almost never equal to each other, so it's worth being extra careful not to mix them up.

faqs.question: What is a one-to-one function?
faqs.answer: A one-to-one function is a function where every output comes from exactly one input — no two different x-values are ever allowed to produce the same y-value. This is a stricter condition than just being a function (which only requires one output per input); one-to-one additionally requires that outputs never repeat.

faqs.question: Why does a function need to be one-to-one in order to have an inverse?
faqs.answer: An inverse has to take each output and send it back to exactly one input — but if a function isn't one-to-one, some output value came from two (or more) different inputs, and the inverse wouldn't know which one to send it back to. Without the one-to-one property, the "inverse" wouldn't actually be a function at all, since it would need to map a single input to multiple outputs.

faqs.question: What is the vertical line test, and why does it work?
faqs.answer:
The vertical line test checks whether a graph represents a function at all: if every vertical line you could draw crosses the graph at most once, it's a function. If any vertical line crosses the graph two or more times, it isn't. It works because a vertical line represents a single x-value — if that line crosses the graph more than once, that one x-value has more than one output, which breaks the basic definition of a function (each input gets exactly one output). This is the test from FN1, and it's worth keeping fresh here since the horizontal line test in the next question is its direct mirror image.

This vertical line crosses the curve exactly once, consistent with every other vertical line you could draw — so this graph is a function.

faqs.question: What is the horizontal line test, and how does it relate to the vertical line test from FN1?
faqs.answer:
The horizontal line test checks whether a function is one-to-one: if every horizontal line you could draw crosses the graph at most once, the function is one-to-one. If any horizontal line crosses the graph two or more times, it isn't. This is the direct counterpart to FN1's vertical line test — that one checked whether a graph was a function at all (one output per input); this one checks the mirror-image question (one input per output).

This horizontal line crosses the curve twice, so this function is NOT one-to-one.

faqs.question: How are the domain and range of a function related to the domain and range of its inverse?
faqs.answer: They swap. Whatever was the domain of the original function becomes the range of the inverse, and whatever was the range of the original function becomes the domain of the inverse. This makes sense given what an inverse does — since it reverses inputs and outputs, it makes sense that it also reverses which set is the domain and which is the range.

faqs.question: How do I determine if a function is one-to-one from its graph?
faqs.answer: Apply the horizontal line test: imagine sliding a horizontal line up and down across the entire graph. If it ever touches the graph in more than one place at the same time, the function is not one-to-one. If every horizontal line touches at most once, the function is one-to-one.

faqs.question: How do I find the inverse of a simple function by reversing the operations in opposite order?
faqs.answer:
List out, in order, every operation the function performs on x. Then reverse both the order AND each individual operation (addition becomes subtraction, multiplication becomes division, and so on).
Worked Example

\( f(x) = \dfrac{x-5}{3} \)

Order of operations on x: subtract 5, then divide by 3.

Reverse, in opposite order: multiply by 3, then add 5.

\( f^{-1}(x) = 3x+5 \)

faqs.question: How do I find the inverse of a function using the swap-x-and-y method?
faqs.answer:
Rewrite f(x) as y, swap x and y everywhere in the equation, then solve the new equation for y. This method works for any function, including more complicated ones where the "reverse the operations" trick from faq-8 gets difficult to track.
Worked Example

\( h(x) = \dfrac{x}{x+1} \) → \( y = \dfrac{x}{x+1} \)

Swap x and y: \( x = \dfrac{y}{y+1} \)

Clear the denominator: \( x(y+1) = y \)

Distribute and gather y-terms: \( xy+x=y \) → \( x = y-xy \) → \( x=y(1-x) \)

Solve for y: \( h^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x}{1-x} \)

faqs.question: How do I verify that two functions are actually inverses of each other?
faqs.answer:
Compose them both ways — check that f(g(x)) simplifies to x, AND that g(f(x)) simplifies to x. If both compositions collapse down to just x, you've confirmed they're truly inverses. If either one doesn't simplify to x, they aren't.
Worked Example

Let \( f(x)=2x+7 \) and \( g(x)=\dfrac{x-7}{2} \).

\( f(g(x)) = 2\left(\dfrac{x-7}{2}\right)+7 = (x-7)+7 = x \) ✓

\( g(f(x)) = \dfrac{(2x+7)-7}{2} = \dfrac{2x}{2} = x \) ✓

Both simplify to x, so f and g are confirmed inverses.

faqs.question: What does it mean to "restrict the domain" of a function so it has an inverse?
faqs.answer: If a function fails the horizontal line test over its full domain, you can sometimes chop off part of the domain so that what's left DOES pass the horizontal line test. You're not changing the function's rule — you're just agreeing to only look at part of its graph, specifically a piece where it behaves one-to-one.

faqs.question: How do I find the inverse of a function whose domain has been restricted, like f(x) = x² for x ≥ 0?
faqs.answer:
Find the inverse using either method from faq-8 or faq-9 as usual — the restriction doesn't change the algebra. The restriction just tells you which piece of the original graph you're working with, which becomes important when stating the inverse's own domain (remember, from faq-6, the original function's range becomes the inverse's domain).
Worked Example

\( f_0(x)=x^2 \), restricted to \( x \geq 0 \)

Swap and solve: \( x=y^2 \) → \( y=\sqrt{x} \) (taking only the positive root, matching the restriction)

\( f_0^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{x} \)

faqs.question: How does the composition skill from FN5 connect to verifying inverse functions?
faqs.answer: Verifying an inverse (faq-10) is literally just function composition from FN5, applied in a specific way — you're composing f and g in both directions and checking whether you get x back. Every skill you built evaluating and simplifying compositions in FN5 is exactly what you need to confirm two functions are truly inverses.

faqs.question: Why do inverse functions matter beyond just "undoing" another function?
faqs.answer: Inverse functions show up constantly whenever you need to reverse a process — converting units back and forth, solving for an original input when you only know the output, or working backward through a real-world model. Later in the course, you'll meet specific inverse function pairs that are foundational to precalculus: logarithms are defined as the inverse of exponential functions, and inverse trigonometric functions let you work backward from a ratio to an angle.

guided.title: Understand the Undo Relationship
guided.prompt: I'm learning about inverse functions. Give me a simple function and its inverse, and help me see step by step how plugging a number through the original function and then through the inverse brings me back to where I started. Then give me a new function and ask me to predict what its inverse would need to do before I calculate it.

guided.title: Practice the Horizontal Line Test
guided.prompt: I'm learning to determine if a function is one-to-one using the horizontal line test. Describe a few different function graphs to me in words (don't just show me images), and ask me to predict whether each one would pass or fail the horizontal line test, and explain my reasoning before you confirm the answer.

guided.title: Practice Both Inverse-Finding Methods
guided.prompt: I'm learning two methods for finding an inverse function: reversing the operations in opposite order, and the swap-x-and-y method. Give me a simple function and walk me through finding its inverse using the reverse-operations method. Then give me a more complex function (like a rational function) and walk me through the swap-x-and-y method instead, explaining why that method works better here.

guided.title: Practice Verifying Inverses
guided.prompt: I'm learning to verify that two functions are inverses by checking that f(g(x)) = x and g(f(x)) = x. Give me a pair of functions that ARE inverses and walk me through verifying it. Then give me a pair that are NOT actually inverses, and help me see where the composition breaks down.

guided.title: Explore Restricting the Domain
guided.prompt: I'm learning why some functions, like f(x) = x^2, need their domain restricted before they can have an inverse. Help me understand why the full function fails the horizontal line test, then walk me through how restricting the domain to x ≥ 0 fixes this, and help me find the resulting inverse function.

paths.label: FN6: Inverse Functions
paths.intro: Builds to the FN6 check: finding the inverse of a function with an odd power or root, or of a rational function.

stages.desc: Two quick algebra skills FN6 leans on. Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Undo powers and roots
stops.target: Undo an odd power with the matching root, and a root with the matching power: \(u^3 = v\) means \(u = \sqrt[3]{v} = v^{1/3}\).
stops.coldPlain: Solve for x: (a) y = x^3, (b) y = x^(1/5).
stops.coldA: (a) \(x = \sqrt[3]{y} = y^{1/3}\). (b) Raise both sides to the 5th power: \(x = y^5\).
stops.solution: (a) A cube is undone by a cube root: x = y^(1/3). (b) A fifth root is undone by a fifth power: x = y^5.
stops.reflect: What undoes a cube? What undoes a fifth root?

stops.title: Solve for x when x appears twice
stops.target: Solve an equation like \(y = \dfrac{x + 4}{x - 2}\) for \(x\): clear the fraction, move all \(x\) terms to one side, factor out \(x\), and divide.
stops.solution: Distribute: 2xy + 3y = 5x - 1. Get every x term on one side: 2xy - 5x = -3y - 1. Factor out x: x(2y - 5) = -3y - 1. Divide: x = (-3y - 1)/(2y - 5).
stops.mistake: Trying to divide by x, or leaving x on both sides of the equation.
stops.reflect: Why is factoring out \(x\) the key step?

stages.desc: The FN6 check asks for one inverse, of one of two types. These stops build up to both.

stops.title: What an inverse does
stops.target: The inverse \(f^{-1}\) undoes \(f\): if \(f(a) = b\), then \(f^{-1}(b) = a\). It swaps inputs and outputs.
stops.coldPlain: Suppose f(2) = 7 and f(-1) = 3. Find f^(-1)(7) and f^(-1)(3).
stops.solution: f sends 2 to 7, so f^(-1) sends 7 back to 2. f sends -1 to 3, so f^(-1) sends 3 back to -1. The point (2, 7) on f becomes (7, 2) on f^(-1).
stops.again: Let \(f(x) = 2x + 5\). Find \(f(3)\), and use it to find \(f^{-1}(11)\).
stops.reflect: Why is \(f^{-1}(x)\) not the same as \(\dfrac{1}{f(x)}\)?

stops.title: Swap and solve
stops.target: Find \(f^{-1}(x)\): write \(y = f(x)\), swap \(x\) and \(y\), then solve for \(y\).
stops.solution: Write y = 3x - 7. Swap x and y: x = 3y - 7. Solve for y: x + 7 = 3y, so y = (x + 7)/3. That y is f^(-1)(x).
stops.mistake: Solving for x without swapping, which gives the right steps but the wrong variable.
stops.reflect: Why does swapping \(x\) and \(y\) turn a function into its inverse?

stops.title: Inverses with odd powers and roots
stops.target: Find the inverse of \(f(x) = a + (x + b)^r\), where \(r\) is an odd power or root: swap, isolate the power, undo it, then isolate \(y\).
stops.solution: Swap: x = 2 + (y - 3)^5. Subtract 2: x - 2 = (y - 3)^5. Undo the 5th power with a 5th root: (x - 2)^(1/5) = y - 3. Add 3: y = (x - 2)^(1/5) + 3. Notice the operations are undone in reverse order.
stops.mistake: Taking the root before subtracting 2, or undoing the 5th power by dividing by 5.
stops.reflect: Why do you undo the operations in the reverse of the order they were done?

stops.title: Inverses of rational functions
stops.target: Find the inverse of \(f(x) = \dfrac{ax + b}{cx + d}\): swap, clear the fraction, collect the \(y\) terms, factor out \(y\), and divide.
stops.solution: Swap: x = (2y + 3)/(y - 5). Multiply both sides by (y - 5): xy - 5x = 2y + 3. Put the y terms on one side: xy - 2y = 5x + 3. Factor out y: y(x - 2) = 5x + 3. Divide: y = (5x + 3)/(x - 2).
stops.mistake: Forgetting to multiply the whole left side by (y - 5), or not factoring y out.
stops.reflect: Which "Get ready" stop does this skill use, and how?

stops.title: Check your inverse
stops.target: Check an inverse by composing: if \(f(f^{-1}(x)) = x\), your inverse is right.
stops.cold: Check that \(f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x + 7}{3}\) is the inverse of \(f(x) = 3x - 7\).
stops.coldPlain: Check that f^(-1)(x) = (x + 7)/3 is the inverse of f(x) = 3x - 7.
stops.solution: Plug f^(-1)(x) into f: f((x + 7)/3) = 3(x + 7)/3 - 7 = x + 7 - 7 = x. Since the result is exactly x, the inverse is correct.
stops.mistake: Plugging in a single number and stopping. A number check is a good start, but composing proves it.
stops.again: Check that \(g(x) = (x - 2)^{1/5} + 3\) is the inverse of \(f(x) = 2 + (x - 3)^5\).
stops.reflect: How can you use this check on the real CheckIt?

stages.desc: A practice check with both types of functions the FN6 CheckIt can give.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: Find the inverse of an odd-power or odd-root function and of a rational function, the way the FN6 check asks.
stops.cold:
Find the inverse of each function.
(a) \(h(x) = -5 + (x + 7)^{1/3}\)
(b) \(f(x) = \dfrac{7x - 2}{3x + 1}\)
stops.coldPlain: Find the inverse of each function: (a) h(x) = -5 + (x + 7)^(1/3), (b) f(x) = (7x - 2)/(3x + 1).
stops.solution: (a) Swap: x = -5 + (y + 7)^(1/3). Add 5: x + 5 = (y + 7)^(1/3). Cube: (x + 5)^3 = y + 7. Subtract 7: y = (x + 5)^3 - 7. (b) Swap: x = (7y - 2)/(3y + 1). Multiply: 3xy + x = 7y - 2. Collect y terms: 3xy - 7y = -x - 2. Factor: y(3x - 7) = -x - 2. Divide: y = (-x - 2)/(3x - 7).
stops.mistake: In (b), moving terms but forgetting to factor out y; in (a), undoing the cube root before adding 5.
stops.again:
Find the inverse of each function.
(a) \(g(x) = 3 + (x - 1)^7\)
(b) \(f(x) = \dfrac{x + 5}{-2x + 3}\)
stops.reflect: Which type (roots/powers or rational) do you want more practice with?
